verdicts.summary: Lean has a stronger form of it. Term for term at viscosity one the two are the same inequality: l2Sq u T = ∫‖u(T,x)‖² = ‖u(t)‖₂²; dissipation u t = Σ_{i<3} ∫‖∂_i u(t,·)‖² = ‖∇u(t)‖₂²; cumulativeForceNorm f T = ∫₀^T ‖f(s)‖₂ ds = F(t); the range T ∈ Ico 0 1 is the paper's 0 ≤ t < 1; the factor 2 on the dissipation and the square on the right are the same. The Lean is more general in one respect: it carries a viscosity ν > 0 and reads 2·ν·∫ dissipation, so the paper's (10.13) is the instance ν = 1 (the paper's Section 10.3 works at viscosity one, cf. Lemma 10.5). One hypothesis difference, recorded rather than charged: the Lean assumes the bundle CandidateProperties ν, one field of which (energy_bounded : UniformFiniteEnergy (Ico 0 1) u) is the uniform kinetic-energy boundedness that the paper states as a consequence of this lemma ('In particular…'). This is not circular as written: the proof text of candidate_energy_dissipation_le and of the lemma it calls, candidate_l2Norm_le_cumulativeForceNorm (IntegratedDissipation.lean:143), uses only smoothness, support, zero datum, divergence-freeness and the equation, never hc.energy_bounded; and NavierStokesR3.CompactEnergy.uniform_finite_energy (CompactEnergy.lean:343) proves that field from the same data, which is how ActualCandidate.of_localized_fields (ActualCandidate.lean:119) discharges it. theorem_1_1_with_dissipation states the inequality for the constructed fields with no candidate hypothesis at all.
